newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Software bug causes HK bourse's Thursday glitch.
newsitem.headline: Software bug causes HK bourse's Thursday glitch.

text.p: A software bug in a file backup-restore macro was responsible for Thursday's erroneous quotations of previous closing prices shown on the Hong Kong stock exchange's computer screens, the exchange said on Friday.

In the unprecedented glitch, the misquotes caused the blue-chip Hang Seng Index to appear to plunge about 515 points or nearly four percent in the opening minutes of Thursday trade, although most traders said they figured out those were mistakes.

The exchange had replaced the faulty software in its Automatic Order Matching and Execution computer system, and would commisison an independent consultant to review the entire system, chief executive Paul Chow told a news conference.
He admitted there was room for improvement in the prevention of such slips, and the exchange would seek to improve.
But he stopped short of guaranteeing similar faults would never occur again, saying "no system is 100 percent perfect."
The executive declined to say if the incident could tarnish the exchange's image internationally, adding however that similar malfuctioning had been seen in other Asian-Pacific bourses.
Chow said he did not believe there had been any attempt to sabotage the exchange's present computer system, which came into operation in 1993.

"The exchange's initial review also indicated that there were areas for improvement in communications between the exchange and Hang Seng Index Services Ltd in respect of our suport in the compilation of the Hang Seng Index," he said.
Hang Seng Index Services is charged with calculating the Hang Seng Index based on prices provided by the stock exchange.
"The exchange is in contact with Hang Seng Index Services Ltd to discuss this matter," Chow added.
The bourse had received three complaints on deals worth a combined HK$500,000 made on Thursday, a day that saw a total of about 69,000 transactions including some 39,000 in the morning.
One of the complaints related to a deal made five hours after the market opened, which was well after the exchange had advised players of the inaccuracy, Chow said.
He added that the complaints were now being reviewed, but declined to say if the complainants could get compensation.
Chow defended the exchange's decision not to suspend the market on Thursday upon discovery of the technical defect.

"The exchange found that the defect was unrelated to and would not affect the functionality of the trading system," he said. "In order to protect the best interests of all stock and futures markets investors, the exchange decided that the normal operation of the stock market should not be disrupted."
The bourse had informed market players of the inaccuracy in good time and advised them where to get correct data, he stressed.
